title: Certified Robustness to Adversarial Examples with Differential Privacy (PixelDP)
authors: Mathias Lecuyer, Vaggelis Atlidakis, Roxana Geambasu, Daniel Hsu, Suman Jana

pages.title: From empirical to certified robustness
pages.subtitle: A defense that comes with a mathematical guarantee

blocks.html: The point of this page: almost every defense against adversarial examples is empirical — it makes today's attacks fail but offers no promise against tomorrow's. History (see the obfuscated-gradients paper in this collection) shows such defenses get broken again and again. PixelDP instead offers a certified defense: a mathematical proof that no perturbation below some size can change the prediction, however clever the attacker.

Shared vocabulary (recurring across this collection). An adversarial example is an input $x' = x + \delta$ where the perturbation $\delta$ is tiny — often invisible — yet flips the prediction. Its size is measured by a norm: the $\ell_2$ norm $\|\delta\|_2$ caps the total Euclidean length of the change, the $\ell_\infty$ norm caps each pixel's change. A certificate is a guaranteed radius $L$ such that every $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_p \le L$ leaves the prediction unchanged.

The surprising tool: differential privacy (DP). DP was invented for a completely different purpose — to keep a single database record from swinging the result of an analysis. PixelDP reuses the same mathematics to keep a single small change in the input pixels from swinging the network's output. The analogy is exact: “one record changes” becomes “the input moves by at most $L$.”
We establish a connection between robustness against adversarial examples and differential privacy ... a randomized function that is DP with respect to small input changes is certifiably robust.

Why it matters. The result scales to large networks and datasets — including ImageNet, a first for certified defenses — works with standard architectures, and gives a per-prediction certificate: for this specific input, the label is guaranteed not to change under any attack within radius $L$.

pages.title: Why empirical defenses keep failing
pages.subtitle: The arms race and how to step out of it

blocks.html: The intuition. An adversarial example is an input $x' = x + \delta$ with $\|\delta\|_p$ tiny, crafted so the prediction flips. Empirical defenses raise the bar against current attacks but leave a nagging question: is the model truly robust, or did we just not find the attack that breaks it? PGD adversarial training (Madry et al.) is strong but still empirical; defensive distillation looked strong and was demolished by C&W. The arms race never ends.

A concrete analogy. An empirical defense is like a lock that has survived every burglar who's tried it so far — reassuring, but no proof. A certificate is like a mathematical theorem that the lock cannot be picked with tools smaller than a certain size. The first depends on who has attacked you; the second depends on nothing.

What a certified defense returns. For a given input it returns not just a label but a guaranteed radius $L$: every perturbation with $\|\delta\|_p \le L$ is proven to leave the prediction unchanged. No future attack inside that ball can ever succeed — the guarantee quantifies over all possible attackers at once, not a fixed list.

What DP normally does. A randomized function is differentially private if changing one input record barely changes its output distribution. Formally, for any two inputs differing by the allowed amount, the probability of any output changes by at most a factor $e^\epsilon$ (plus a slack $\delta$). The practical effect: the output is stable — no single record can swing it much.

PixelDP's leap. Treat a norm-bounded change in the input image as the “one record change” of DP. If the network's class scores are differentially private with respect to a change of size $L$ in the input, then those scores cannot move much when the input is perturbed within the $L$-ball — and if the scores can't move much, the argmax (the predicted class) is stable. That stability is exactly what becomes a robustness certificate.

pages.title: Inject calibrated noise into the network
pages.subtitle: Making the score function differentially private

blocks.html: The idea. An ordinary network is deterministic, so it can't be DP. PixelDP makes it DP by inserting a noise layer: Gaussian (or Laplace) noise is added at some point in the forward pass, calibrated so the mapping from input to class scores satisfies $(\epsilon, \delta)$-DP with respect to a change of size up to $L$ in the chosen input norm. The noise is what buys the stability.

Where the noise goes. It can be added to the input itself, or after the first layer(s). The earlier it sits, the simpler the sensitivity analysis; placing it deeper (after some learned layers) often preserves more accuracy. Either way, the layers before the noise are what determine how a $\delta$-sized input change propagates.

How much noise: the calibration. The amount depends on the sensitivity $\Delta$ — how much the pre-noise output can change when the input moves by $L$. For Gaussian noise providing $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP at attack bound $L$, the standard deviation scales as:

Term by term: $\sigma$ is the noise standard deviation; $L$ is the attack radius you want to certify; $\Delta_2$ is the $\ell_2$ sensitivity (how strongly a unit input change propagates to the noise layer — computed from the network's structure/Lipschitz bound); $\epsilon$ and $\delta$ are the DP privacy budget ($\epsilon$ the multiplicative slack, $\delta$ a tiny failure probability). The $\sqrt{2\ln(1.25/\delta)}$ factor is the standard Gaussian-mechanism constant from DP.

Reading it plainly. A bigger guaranteed radius $L$, or a more sensitive network ($\Delta_2$ large), demands more noise; a tighter privacy budget (smaller $\epsilon$) also demands more noise. Noise is the currency you spend to buy a stability guarantee — and spending it costs clean accuracy.

At prediction time. Because the network is now random, PixelDP runs it many times (Monte Carlo) on the same input and averages the scores, producing an estimated expected score $\hat{\mathbb{E}}[\,Q_k(x)\,]$ for each class $k$. Those expectations are what the certificate is built on.

pages.title: From DP to a robustness certificate
pages.subtitle: The bound that does the work

blocks.html: The bridge: expected-output stability. DP has a corollary that is the heart of the whole method. If a function's output lies in $[0,1]$ and the function is $(\epsilon,\delta)$-DP for input changes up to $L$, then for any perturbation within that bound the expected score cannot jump by more than a controlled factor:

Term by term: $Q_k(\cdot)$ is the (randomized) score for class $k$, valued in $[0,1]$; $\mathbb{E}[Q_k(x)]$ is its expected value on the clean input; $\mathbb{E}[Q_k(x+\delta)]$ on the attacked input; $e^\epsilon$ is the multiplicative drift allowed by the DP budget and $\delta$ the additive slack. In words: the DP guarantee literally caps how far any class score can move when the attacker perturbs the input inside the $L$-ball.

The certificate. Let $k_1$ be the top-scoring class and $k_2$ the runner-up. The prediction is certified robust at this input if the top score, even after its worst allowed drop, still beats the runner-up after its worst allowed rise:

Term by term: the left side is the clean top-class score; the right side is the worst-case runner-up score after drift — the $e^{2\epsilon}$ factor accounts for $k_1$ dropping and $k_2$ rising (each by $e^\epsilon$), and $(1+e^\epsilon)\delta$ collects the additive slacks. If this strict inequality holds, no $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_p \le L$ can make $k_2$ overtake $k_1$.

What happens when it fails. If the inequality does not hold, PixelDP simply abstains from certifying that input — it still outputs a label, but makes no robustness promise. It never makes a false guarantee. This is why robustness becomes a measurable, per-input quantity rather than a blanket hope.
The robustness certificate is computed at prediction time, on a per-example basis.

pages.title: Making the bound trustworthy in practice
pages.subtitle: Monte Carlo estimation and confidence intervals

blocks.html: The subtlety. The certificate is stated in terms of true expectations $\mathbb{E}[Q_k(x)]$, but PixelDP can only estimate them by sampling the noisy network a finite number of times. A naive plug-in of the sample means would make the guarantee probabilistic in a sloppy way. The fix is to be conservative.

Confidence bounds. Using Hoeffding's inequality (a tail bound for averages of bounded random variables), PixelDP computes a high-probability interval for each expected score, then plugs the pessimistic ends into the certificate check — the lower bound for the top class, the upper bound for the runner-up. This guarantees the certificate holds with high probability $(1-\alpha)$ despite using sampled scores.

items: Lower-bound the top class's expected score (assume it's as small as the data allows).
Upper-bound the runner-up's expected score (assume it's as large as the data allows).
Certify only if the conservative top still dominates the conservative runner-up under the DP drift bound.
More Monte Carlo samples shrink the confidence intervals and certify more inputs.

blocks.html: The accuracy–robustness knob. The whole trade-off appears as a single dial: more noise ($\sigma$ up) yields a larger certified radius $L$ but lowers clean accuracy (the noise blurs real signal). PixelDP lets you set this explicitly, with the guarantee always intact — a transparent version of the same accuracy–robustness tension the robust-features paper explains at the level of the data.

Why it matters. A guarantee you can only estimate is worthless unless the estimation is sound. The Hoeffding wrapper is what turns “we sampled and it looked fine” into “with probability $1-\alpha$, this prediction is provably robust to radius $L$.”

pages.title: Scales where prior certified defenses could not
pages.subtitle: ImageNet-scale certificates

blocks.html: The scaling win. Earlier certified defenses relied on exact verification or convex relaxations — precise, but they choked on anything bigger than small networks and datasets. PixelDP's noise-based approach is architecture-agnostic and cheap (just add a noise layer and sample), so it certifies robustness on large models and on datasets up to ImageNet — a first at that scale for a certified method.

items: Gives a genuine guarantee, not just empirical resistance to today's attacks.
Works as a wrapper around standard architectures with a single added noise layer.
The certificate is per-input, so you know exactly which predictions are provably safe and which the model declines to certify.
Trades clean accuracy for certified radius via the noise level — transparently, with the guarantee always intact.

blocks.html: How to read a certified-accuracy number. “Certified accuracy at radius $L$” means: the fraction of test inputs that are both classified correctly and certified robust to every $\delta$ with $\|\delta\|_p \le L$. It is a strictly harder, more honest metric than clean accuracy or even empirical robust accuracy — it counts only predictions backed by a proof.

The lasting contribution. Conceptually, PixelDP showed that differential privacy and adversarial robustness are two faces of the same stability requirement — both are about an output that doesn't move much when the input moves a little. That bridge directly seeded randomized smoothing, which sharpened the noise-based certificate into one of the most reliable and widely used tools in adversarial ML.

How it connects. Where FGSM and C&W built attacks, PGD/Madry built a strong empirical defense, and obfuscated gradients showed how easily empirical defenses fool us, PixelDP is the answer to “can we ever prove robustness?” — trading some accuracy and some certified radius for a guarantee that holds against every attacker, named or not.
